body: Oil Traders Want U.S. to Release Sanctioned Tankers as Freight Costs Soar What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have prompted an increase in EV sales to avoid retail fuel inflation and gas demand destruction in favor of other power generation sources. With COP31 starting next week, some participants have signaled that faster electrification could become the focus of the event. “I would like to see a strong outcome on electrification in our presidency-led decision,” this year’s COP’s head of negotiations, Australian climate change minister Chris Bowen, told Bloomberg. Bowen also said he would consider COP31 a success if all participating countries made a commitment to increase the share of electricity in their final energy demand mix. Final energy is the kind that is actually used, as opposed to primary energy, which is energy in its raw form. While crude oil, for instance, is primary energy, gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel are final energy. Electricity is also a form of final energy, with its primary input coming from primary coal, gas, water, geothermal, and, more recently, solar and wind energy. It is those two latter sources of energy that COP leaders have selected as favorites for the grid of the near and far future—but have so far failed to make dominant. The world still sources over 80% of its primary energy from hydrocarbons. In other words, over 80% of the energy resources that the world consumes come from oil, gas, and coal. But, according to Bloomberg’s Zero podcast host, Akshat Rathi, by the time the energy goes from primary to final, the share of hydrocarbons falls to 65%. “Thus electrification is foremost an energy efficiency solution, because it reduces primary energy demand without cutting the useful outcomes that citizens want,” Rathi wrote in a recent report on COP31 ambitions. Electrification is the ultimate goal of the energy transition in every industry and aspect of life, excluding, perhaps chemicals production and related fields that rely on hydrocarbon feedstock for their output. Yet it is not just any electrification, of course, that transition advocates promote. Electrification must come from wind, solar, biomass, geothermal, hydro, and nuclear if it is to be done the right way, in view of emission reduction targets agreed a decade ago in Paris. Related: The Iran War Isn't Over, but Oil Traders Are Already Pricing In Peace Over these past ten years, trillions have been invested in the goal of electrification. Indeed, transition investment just last year hit $2.3 trillion, according to BloombergNEF . This was 8% higher than total transition investment during the previous year—and there was not even a war in the Middle East to cause the most serious disruption to oil and gas supply in history. The biggest portion of that total went into transport electrification, and the second-biggest portion went into wind and solar capacity. The buildout in electric vehicles, wind, and solar generation capacity and related technologies over the past 10 years has been quite impressive. It has failed to reduce global emissions of carbon dioxide, but it has led to regional declines, for instance in Europe, by means of energy demand destruction, mostly by discouragement through higher costs resulting from emission reduction policies. Bessent says 'not necessarily' a mistake if the Fed hikes again
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent joined CNBC for an interview on Oct. 28, 2026.
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday that further Federal Reserve rate hikes wouldn't necessarily be a mistake. After CNBC's Brian Sullivan asked if rate increases in the future would constitute a monetary policy error, Bessent responded: "That's not necessarily so." Bessent's comments came hours after the Fed announced it would keep interest rates unchanged at its October gathering, as the market widely expected. Bessent is a key confidant of President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly called for lower interest rates. Trump pressured Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's predeccesor, Jerome Powell, over the issue during Powell's final months at the helm of the central bank. But Bessent said Wednesday that both he and Trump believe Warsh is doing well and can strike a balance between ensuring full employment and stable prices. "I think Chair Warsh is off to a great start," Bessent said. "As I often say, I have great confidence in him." The Fed's decision to hold rates steady came a month after it lifted borrowing costs for the first time in three years. Fed funds futures traders widely expected the central bank to return to rate hiking when it meets again in December. Bessent said he would like to see the Fed have an "open mind" about the supply shock from energy prices having a "transitory nature." The U.S. war with Iran has led to a sharp drop in global crude production volumes, in turn leading annual inflation readings to move further from the Fed's target of 2%. Bessent also said the U.S. efforts to isolate the Iran economy, dubbed Operation Economic Outcast , have been "very successful." He said internal estimates show that Iran's economy could contract by as much as 25% in the span of a year. When asked about bond yields on artificial-intelligence related debt, the Wall Street veteran said "we monitor" it, but that it didn't need to cause concern. Bessent specifically referenced neoclouds , a type of company providing specific cloud infrastructure supporting AI that has recently struggled in the market. Tesla CEO Elon Musk warned on Sunday that more than 200 neocloud firms "are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation." "I don't think it's problematic at all," Bessent said. "The neoclouds are a small component of the overall ecosystem, and we're still seeing the financing getting done. We're still seeing the deals get done." Bessent told CNBC he expects the third-quarter GDP data expected Thursday to be "strong." But he clarified that "I haven't seen it yet."

title: The UK cuts energy bills, taxes banks and boosts defense in high-stakes budget
summary: The U.K. budget cuts household energy costs, raises taxes on banks and directs billions toward defense, Ukraine and artificial intelligence
body: The U.K.'s finance minister John Healey delivered his first fiscal budget on Wednesday, announcing funding for defense, AI initiatives and measures designed to ease cost-of-living pressures. The Autumn Budget included dozens of measures aimed largely at easing rising costs for Britain's population, but Healey was careful not to risk the ire of markets, which responded broadly positively to his plans. As a net energy importer, the U.K. is vulnerable to external energy shocks. Inflation has risen sharply this year, with surging fuel costs driving the annual inflation rate to 3.5% in September. Markets expect the Bank of England to hike interest rates next month, while government borrowing costs have risen sharply this year. The U.K. government, led by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, had promised to alleviate economic pressures ahead of the budget. On Wednesday, Healey said he would deliver "breathing space" for families, saying the country needs "radical change on energy," and citing the inflationary impact of the U.S.-Iran war — a conflict he said "we did not want." His measures included the removal of standing charges on household gas heating bills, the extension of a tax break on electricity for millions of households through July 2027, and £100 ($133) checks for those living in the four lowest local housing tax bands. This will cost £2.6 billion. Healey said tariffs would be removed on over 100 grocery products, a policy announced before the budget was officially unveiled. Small business relief from business rates — a tax on commercial premises — would be extended to include more companies in the hospitality, retail and leisure sectors. Other measures included £15 million to provide books for children, funding aimed at reducing homelessness and support for people to purchase their first home. The U.K.'s minimum wage will rise by 3.9%, while a planned cut to tax-free savings thresholds was canceled. But Healey also pledged to bring down the welfare bill, pointing to reforms to pensions and sickness benefits. But he said he would not "write off a million young people [or] see disabled people suffer the indignities of a system that has been found 'not fit for purpose.'" The U.K.'s welfare bill, which reached 10.7% of UK GDP in 2024/25, has been a contentious issue in recent years. Previous finance minister Rachel Reeves watered down her own plans to cut welfare spending after a rebellion from lawmakers within her party. Healey also announced investments in developing — and regulating — the U.K.'s artificial intelligence industry. "Nowhere is the necessary role for the state clearer than in artificial intelligence," he said, as he announced hundreds of millions of pounds in funding for AI security and sovereignty. He announced a "covenant" for data centers in the country, with "strict tests" they must meet: "To invest in local communities, create local jobs and protect local water supplies. In return, critical data centers will get the grid connections they need, and, where necessary, be allowed to build onsite generation while they wait," Healey said. Healey also announced tax breaks for founders, including a reduced capital gains tax rate on gains of up to £10 million. Cash would also be injected into various regional hubs, Healey said, to "unleash Britain's innovation power." The budget also included £10 billion of additional economic and military support for Ukraine . "Today we send a clear message to Moscow: Britain will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes," he said. More funding would go to defense, he added, to ensure the country can meet its NATO spending commitments. "At the Spending Review next year, I confirm that I will set out the details of how we will meet our NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030," he said. body: Shares of SpaceX (SPCX) could nearly double as its Nvidia-powered AI expansion opens up a larger revenue opportunity, Oppenheimer says. SPCX stock fell 1% on Wednesday to $140.71, logging its second consecutive session in the red. Oppenheimer raised its SpaceX price target to $280 from $250, implying a 99% upside from current levels, and maintained its ‘Outperform’ rating. The firm identified SpaceX’s vertically integrated AI platform as a key differentiator. According to a report on Investing.com, the research firm said that the company owns valuable data, has access to substantial capital and Nvidia GPUs, and can build infrastructure rapidly. Oppenheimer said new Nvidia Rubin chips could pay for themselves in one year amid strong AI compute demand and pricing. SpaceX could retain 100% of the revenue generated through Cursor and Grok or capture around 50% when acting as an AI infrastructure wholesaler, the firm said. The Cursor acquisition has also strengthened SpaceX’s agentic coding data and reasoning capabilities, benefiting Grok Bot and Grok 4.6, with further improvements expected in Grok 5.0. Oppenheimer said AI usage and productivity are running ahead of expectations, although infrastructure remains the biggest bottleneck. The firm raised its long-term revenue estimates by about 10% on stronger compute pricing, compounding to 20% over time when combined with higher capex. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Nvidia recently detailed a space-optimized Vera Rubin NVL72 system, targeting initial launches in the fourth quarter of 2027 and significant scaling in 2028. SpaceX’s first-gen Starmind AI1 satellite is designed around an orbital configuration of 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs. SpaceX also adopted standalone Vera CPUs for Grok’s agentic workloads on Earth, making Nvidia’s architecture the backbone of both its terrestrial Colossus-scale builds and orbital computing network. Deepwater’s Gene Munster estimated that SpaceX already contributes nearly $5 billion, or 5%, of Nvidia’s quarterly revenue, up from 3%. SpaceX revealed the scale of its AI ambitions during its first public earnings call last month. Melius Research estimated that even 2 GW of SpaceX’s planned buildout could generate $100 billion in incremental revenue for Nvidia. title: World Bank’s $4,000 Gold Forecast For 2028 Is Already Close To Today’s Price - ascendants.in
body: The World Bank expects gold prices to decline over the next two years, but its latest forecast suggests that much of the anticipated correction may already have taken place. The institution projects gold will average $4,000 per ounce in 2028, a level that is now less than 2% below its latest reported market price. In its Commodity Markets Outlook, released on October 28, the World Bank estimated that gold would average $4,600 per ounce in 2026, representing a 33.6% increase from the previous year’s average of $3,442. However, it expects prices to moderate in the following years, falling 7.6% to $4,250 in 2027 and another 5.9% to $4,000 in 2028. Spot gold closed at $4,068.71 per ounce on Friday, putting the market price remarkably close to the bank’s projection for 2028. The difference is less than $69 per ounce, or approximately 1.7%. The forecast also marks a downward revision from the World Bank’s April estimates, when it projected average gold prices of $4,700 for 2026 and $4,300 for 2027. Although the World Bank’s projections indicate further weakness, gold has already experienced a substantial correction from its recent peak. The metal closed at a record $5,379 per ounce on January 29. At $4,068.71, the latest reported closing price represents a decline of approximately 24.4% from that high. The bank’s $4,000 forecast for 2028 would put prices around 25.6% below the January record. Recent monetary policy developments have contributed to the decline. Higher government bond yields and a stronger US dollar have made gold less attractive to investors, particularly because the precious metal does not generate interest income. The World Bank reported that gold prices declined 5% during the July-September quarter and weakened further in October amid expectations of tighter monetary policy. However, the annual-average nature of the forecast is important. The $4,000 projection does not mean gold will necessarily trade at that level at the end of 2028. Prices could move considerably higher or lower during the year while still producing the projected annual average. The World Bank expects central banks to purchase less gold in 2027 and 2028 than they have in recent years. It also anticipates continued weakness in jewellery demand, which has been declining since 2023. The report noted, “Jewelry demand, by contrast, has declined sharply since 2023 and is expected to remain weak.” Despite these pressures, the institution does not expect global gold demand to collapse. Investment demand and central bank purchases together accounted for approximately half of global gold demand during the first half of 2026. The bank expects these sources of demand to provide continued support to the market over the next two years. “Global gold demand is expected to remain firm over 2027–28,” the report stated. This suggests that although the World Bank anticipates a gradual price correction, continued investor interest and central bank purchases could limit the extent of the decline. The World Bank has identified risks on both sides of its forecast. Escalating geopolitical conflicts or renewed trade tensions could increase demand for gold as a safe-haven asset, pushing prices above the projected levels. Conversely, interest rates remaining higher than expected could put additional pressure on the precious metal. A sustained easing of tensions in the Middle East could also reduce demand for safe-haven investments. Interest rate expectations are particularly important for gold because investors compare its appeal with interest-bearing assets such as government bonds. The outlook could face another test in December. body: The International Monetary Fund has warned that slowing artificial intelligence investment could complicate central banks' efforts to control inflation, as an earlier IMF downside scenario shows US economic output potentially falling 1.8% below expectations by 2028. Speaking in Washington on November 6, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said policymakers would need to consider any weakening in AI-driven growth when setting interest rates. Her comments followed a sharp technology-stock selloff that intensified concerns about the sustainability of enormous AI infrastructure investments. In an October IMF assessment , Georgieva described AI investment as a major source of economic expansion but warned that disappointing returns, leverage and concentrated market exposure could transmit losses across the financial system. The IMF's October World Economic Outlook examined a scenario in which a sharp reversal in AI investment triggers declining asset prices, weaker business spending and slower economic activity. Under that adverse scenario, global GDP could be 1.1% below baseline projections by 2028, with US output 1.8% below its expected level. These figures are not forecasts of outright economic contraction. They measure how much smaller economies could become relative to the IMF's central projections if the investment boom reverses. The risks are particularly relevant to the United States, where AI infrastructure investment has supported construction, semiconductor demand and economic activity. The warning follows a November 5 Nasdaq correction , as investors reassess whether AI companies can generate sufficient profits to justify their infrastructure spending. Artificial intelligence is creating an unusual challenge for monetary policymakers. Building data centers requires enormous investments in electricity, construction materials, semiconductor equipment and computing infrastructure. That spending supports economic growth but can simultaneously increase demand and inflationary pressure. Georgieva said the investment boom was helping some economies offset the negative effects of the Middle East oil-supply shock while also contributing to financial stability concerns. The tension has already attracted attention from Federal Reserve policymakers , who have warned that AI spending could raise costs before promised productivity improvements materialize. If investment slows, economic growth could weaken, potentially creating pressure for lower interest rates. However, persistent energy-related inflation could push central banks toward maintaining restrictive policies. The IMF's concerns extend beyond declining semiconductor share prices. Large technology companies increasingly rely on financing arrangements involving cloud providers, chip manufacturers and AI developers. In October, the IMF warned that hyperscalers' share of global investment-grade bond issuance had risen from less than 1% in 2024 to approximately 10%. That growing borrowing exposure means disappointing AI returns could pressure both stock and credit markets. The vulnerability has become visible in CoreWeave's credit market , where default protection costs have climbed as investors question highly leveraged AI expansion. Meanwhile, technology fund withdrawals illustrate how investors are reassessing exposure even while broader equity markets attract capital. body: Oil Traders Want U.S. to Release Sanctioned Tankers as Freight Costs Soar Haley Zaremba is an energy journalist and researcher with more than a decade of professional experience covering global energy systems, land and natural resources, and… Artificial intelligence companies are deepening their ties with the fossil fuel industries as some of the biggest names in the tech world make massive deals with energy companies, both to power their energy-hungry data centers and to embed machine learning into the energy sector itself. Already, the artificial intelligence boom is causing a natural gas surge in the United States, and experts expect that data center hyperscalers will greatly extend the life of fossil fuels in the global energy mix, even as the world continues to shatter clean energy growth records. This Monday, OpenAI – the firm behind ChatGPT – made a deal with Abu Dhabi's ADNOC “to deploy advanced AI capabilities across the state energy firm's operations,” according to reporting from Reuters. The report noted that the agreement “mark[s] the latest step in the ChatGPT maker's deepening ties with the United Arab Emirates.” But the trend extends far beyond just one firm and one country. Globally, AI firms are racing to make products designed for some of the richest pockets in the world – oil and gas companies. A recent report from nonpartisan global news outlet Semafor notes that the OpenAI-ADNOC deal “was the highest-profile example in a broader push at ADIPEC by tech companies to pitch bespoke, AI-driven tools to help operate drilling rigs, refineries, and other oil assets.” What is more, the deepening ties between AI and fossil fuels goes both ways. Big Tech is planning data centers faster than global power grids can keep up. Plus, legislation under the Trump administration has pushed tech companies to provide their own energy sources to power new planned data centers, leaving Silicon Valley scrambling to add energy production capacity by any means necessary. While this includes funding research and development of next-gen clean energy technologies like nuclear fusion and space-based solar power, in practice it has translated to massive natural gas contracts. At present, Amazon is constructing a gas-fired power plant in Texas that, if completed according to the current plan involving the development of seven natural gas plants, will be the single-biggest source of power-related emissions in the entire United States . In August, AI giant Nvidia announced that it would partner with Japan’s SoftBank and the United States federal government to build the largest fossil-fuel plant in the country in order to power an Ohio project by OpenAI. Microsoft, too, just signed a 20-year deal with Chevron to provide 2.67 gigawatts of natural-gas-fired power for a proposed West Texas data center. AI advocates argue that in the long run, AI will save more energy than it consumes thanks to efficiency gains across all of the sectors that use it. However, those gains are a double-edged sword. A recent paper published by NPJ Climate Action found that, if fossil fuels make economic gains anywhere above zero thanks to AI integration, enabled emissions will exceed avoided emissions. In a scenario where both the fossil fuel and the renewables sector benefit equally from AI gains, global CO2 emissions will still increase by between 0.47 billion tons and 1.8 billion tons a year. “On the smaller side it's about the emissions of Mexico annually,” Holly Alpine, one of the co-authors of the research, was recently quoted by the Wall Street Journal. Despite NPJ Climate Action’s sobering warning, AI firms are tripping over themselves to court fossil fuel companies and secure long-term contracts with economic heavyweights in Big Oil. The OpenAI-ADNOC deal is not the first of its kind, but the high-profile nature of the agreement is indicative of the direction that the sectors as a whole are heading – and it’s not good for anyone’s bottom line but their own.

Global oil prices on Thursday touched their highest level in four years as negotiations between the U.S. and Iran showed little sign of resolving a historic energy crisis . Brent futures, the benchmark index for global oil trading, vaulted as high as $126 a barrel, before dropping to $114 a barrel. Still, that price stands more than 10% higher than it registered five days ago. A separate measure of U.S. oil prices also soared this week, but fell short of multi-year records. The recent surge in oil prices will likely push up gasoline and other fuel costs over the coming days, some analysts told ABC News. Within weeks, they said, the jump in prices could spread to groceries, furniture and just about any other item delivered by diesel-fueled trucks and tankers. Shoppers are already smarting from financial strain, analysts from Edward Jones and EY-Parthenon said. Before this week, oil prices had jumped about 50% since the Iran war broke out on Feb. 28. The energy shock sent overall inflation rising in March. A sustained rise in oil prices "could exacerbate the pressure on U.S. households," James McCann, a senior economist for investment strategy at Edward Jones, said in a statement to ABC News. The Middle East conflict prompted the Iranian closure of the Strait of Hormuz , a maritime trading route that facilitates the transport of about one-fifth of global oil supply. The vast majority of oil that passes through the strait is bound for Asian markets. But since oil prices are set on a global market, prices have climbed for just about everyone as buyers chase fewer barrels of crude. A U.S.-Iran ceasefire has entered its fourth week, averting a resumption of wide hostilities while leaving the strait under Iran's effective control. The U.S. has mounted a blockade of Iran's ports in the strait, squeezing a key source of Iranian government funds derived from oil exports, but exacerbating the global petroleum shortage. The average price of a gallon of gas jumped to $4.30 as of Thursday, hitting its highest level since 2022, AAA data showed. The average price of a gallon of gas is on track to hit $4.50 by next week, which would amount to a nearly 5% jump, De Haan said. The rise in oil prices is also expected to push up the cost of diesel fuel, which powers many of the trucks, trains and ships that transport products across a vast global supply chain. The price hike for any individual item will likely be modest, but the pileup of extra costs could weigh on wallets, analysts previously told ABC News. "Price pressures are expected to intensify through the summer, particularly as higher energy, food and commodities costs feed through," consulting company EY-Parthenon said in a statement on Thursday. The prospect of higher costs comes as price increases for food, transportation and apparel each clock in above the Federal Reserve's target rate of 2%. title: Bank of England hikes rates to 4% as inflation fears mount - https://www.indiagazette.com/
body: LONDON, U.K.: The Bank of England raised interest rates to 4 percent on November 5, its first increase in more than three years, warning that further tightening could be necessary as the US-Iran conflict continues to drive up energy costs and threaten Britain's inflation outlook. The central bank's Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1 to increase its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point from 3.75 percent. The lone dissenter, Catherine Mann, supported a larger half-point increase to 4.25 percent. The decision comes as the bank forecasts inflation will reach approximately 5 percent by the middle of next year, more than twice its 2 percent target, creating further cost-of-living challenges for Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government. "Today's increase shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes. But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase," Governor Andrew Bailey said. Although the bank has seen limited evidence of accelerating inflation outside sectors directly affected by higher energy costs, policymakers concluded that months of elevated prices had created sufficient future inflationary pressure to justify immediate action. Consumer price inflation reached 3.5 percent in September, raising concerns among some policymakers that inflation expectations could become harder to control. Mann, who had previously criticised the bank for being too slow to reassure markets about inflation, cited "non-linear inflation risks" and warned of a possible loss of confidence in the central bank. Financial markets had widely anticipated Thursday's increase and were pricing in three further quarter-point hikes during 2027, more than most economists expect. Bailey said the difference reflected financial markets accounting for the possibility of a sharper rise in energy prices, while economists generally based their forecasts on a more moderate tightening cycle. "Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates," he said in the policy minutes. Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli also indicated that another increase would probably be needed in the near term. External policymaker Megan Greene called for "further tightening", while Chief Economist Huw Pill referred to the need for "additional hikes". However, policymakers Swati Dhingra and Alan Taylor said they would require stronger evidence of secondary inflationary effects before supporting additional increases. Alongside the rate decision, the Bank of England upgraded its economic growth forecasts for this year and next to 1.6 percent and 1.3 percent, respectively, exceeding projections issued by the government's Office for Budget Responsibility last week. The bank attributed some of the stronger outlook to investment in artificial intelligence and a modest temporary boost from Finance Minister John Healey's annual budget. Under its central forecast, inflation is expected to peak at an average of 4.8 percent in the second quarter of 2027. In a more adverse scenario, with oil prices reaching approximately $130 a barrel instead of around $100, inflation could climb to 6.2 percent in the third quarter of 2027. The bank now expects inflation to return to its 2 percent target only in the third quarter of 2028, six months later than it projected in July. It also forecast that British households' income from work, after accounting for inflation and taxes, would decline both this year and next. The government's latest budget is expected to reduce inflation by 0.25 percentage points at its peak, although the bank warned that inflation could rise again when temporary cost-of-living support measures expire.
